description: The eukaryotic model organism discussed in the review as the biological system in which peroxisome biogenesis and protein import are studied. It serves as the subject/population for understanding intracellular targeting mechanisms and organelle-specific protein trafficking.

Intracellular organelles in yeast that possess specific enzymes and perform specialized metabolic functions. They are the focal organelle for the paper's discussion of biogenesis and selective protein import.

Membrane-bound cellular compartments in eukaryotic cells that carry out distinct metabolic roles. They provide the broader cellular context for organelle-specific protein targeting and compartmentalization.

The cellular process by which proteins are directed to their correct subcellular destinations. In this text, it is mediated by cis-acting amino acid sequences and recognition by the translocation machinery.

The movement of proteins from the cytosol across membranes into specific organelles. The abstract emphasizes translocation across hydrophobic membrane barriers and into peroxisomes without post-translational modification.
The process of forming and maintaining peroxisomes, including the mechanisms that support import of peroxisomal proteins. It is the central biological topic of the review.

Protein-encoded sequence motifs that function as recognition signals for sorting and translocation. They are described as directing proteins to specific organelles by interacting with the cellular translocation machinery.
Sequence-based molecular signals that enable the cellular machinery to identify proteins for correct subcellular targeting. They are functionally linked to protein sorting and organelle import.
The molecular machinery responsible for recognizing targeting signals and mediating protein movement to organelles. It is implicated in the import of proteins into peroxisomes and other organelles.

A protein trafficking route mentioned as one of the major targeting destinations for proteins with cleavable amino-terminal extensions. It provides a comparative example of organelle-targeting mechanisms.

A major eukaryotic organelle referenced as a destination for proteins targeted by cleavable amino-terminal extensions. It is included as a comparative organelle in the discussion of protein targeting.
A photosynthetic organelle referenced as another destination for proteins targeted by cleavable amino-terminal extensions. It is used as a comparative example of organelle-specific protein import.
The intracellular compartment where proteins are synthesized before being transported to their target organelles. It is the source location for proteins undergoing sorting and translocation.
Membrane interfaces that proteins may need to cross during intracellular targeting. They represent the physical barrier context for translocation into organelles.
A protein processing step that is noted as generally absent for most peroxisomal proteins during import. Its absence distinguishes peroxisomal targeting from other organelle-targeting pathways.
The selective transport of proteins into peroxisomes, which is the specific mechanistic problem addressed by the review. It is central to peroxisome biogenesis in yeast.

A conserved molecular chaperone that supports folding and functional maturation of many client proteins. In this text, Hsp90 is the central molecular feature regulating Candida albicans morphogenesis and virulence, and it is highlighted as a potential therapeutic target.

A broad set of proteins whose folding and function are facilitated by Hsp90. These proteins are described as core hubs of signal transduction networks and are functionally linked to Hsp90-dependent regulation.
Cellular signaling pathways in which many Hsp90 client proteins serve as core hubs. These networks are implicated in the regulation of morphogenesis and virulence in Candida albicans.
An opportunistic fungal pathogen that is also a natural commensal of the human microbiota. It is the organism discussed as the subject of morphogenesis and virulence regulation by Hsp90.
The host-associated microbial environment in which Candida albicans exists as a natural commensal. It provides the ecological context for the organism before invasive disease occurs.
Severe disease outcome caused by fungal pathogens such as Candida albicans. The text identifies Candida albicans as a leading cause of this endpoint, especially in immunocompromised individuals.
A vulnerable population stratum with reduced immune function, in whom Candida albicans is particularly associated with invasive fungal infections.

entity_name: MORPHOGENETIC TRANSITION BETWEEN YEAST AND FILAMENTOUS FORMS
description: The morphological switching process by which Candida albicans transitions between yeast and filamentous states. This process is tightly coupled to disease causation and is regulated by Hsp90.
The pathogenic capacity of Candida albicans to cause disease. In this text, virulence is a key endpoint controlled by Hsp90 and linked to morphogenetic switching.
The fungal Hsp90 protein considered as a therapeutic target. Targeting this agent is proposed as a strategy to combat fungal infections.
A proposed intervention approach aimed at targeting fungal Hsp90 to combat fungal infections. It represents the translational application discussed in the abstract.
Disease outcomes caused by fungal pathogens, including invasive fungal infections. The text frames targeting fungal Hsp90 as a way to combat these infections.

A class of fungal signaling molecules that mediate cell-cell communication and regulate fungal biological activities, including morphogenesis, biofilm development, and pathogenicity. In this review, they are the central molecular features discussed as regulators of fungal behavior.
A fungal quorum-sensing molecule mentioned as one of the specific signaling compounds secreted by fungi to regulate morphology and other behaviors.
A fungal quorum-sensing molecule secreted by fungi and implicated in regulating fungal biological activities and morphogenesis.
A fungal quorum-sensing molecule identified in the text as part of the signaling repertoire used by fungi for cell-cell communication and behavioral control.
A fungal quorum-sensing molecule secreted by fungi that contributes to quorum sensing-mediated regulation of fungal activities.
A fungal species used as an example of a yeast in which quorum-sensing molecules have been studied for effects on morphogenesis and pathogenicity.
A fungal species mentioned as a study example for quorum-sensing molecule effects in yeasts.
A filamentous fungal species cited as an example organism in which quorum-sensing molecules have been studied.
A filamentous fungal species included among the organisms used to study fungal quorum-sensing molecules and their effects.
A fungal species cited as an example in which quorum-sensing molecules have been investigated for roles in morphogenesis and pathogenicity.
The developmental process by which fungi change form, including yeast-to-hypha transition, and a major biological process regulated by quorum-sensing molecules.
A morphogenetic transition in fungi from yeast form to hyphal growth, highlighted as a specific process influenced by quorum-sensing molecules.
A fungal developmental process involving macroconidial germination that is affected by quorum-sensing molecules.
A regulated cell death process in fungi that is induced by quorum-sensing molecules according to the text.
A form of programmed cell death referenced as a fungal response initiated by quorum-sensing molecules.
The disease-causing capacity of fungi, described as being influenced by quorum-sensing molecules and a key endpoint of interest in the review.
The process of biofilm formation and maturation in fungal communities, during which quorum-sensing molecules are produced to regulate population and morphology.
The formation of fungal biofilms, emphasized as a major process controlled by quorum-sensing molecules.
A disease outcome referenced as a target for improved control measures informed by understanding quorum-sensing molecules.

An opportunistic human fungal pathogen used here as the biological subject of the review. It is the organism in which morphogenesis and cell cycle progression are discussed, including yeast, pseudohyphal, and hyphal growth forms.
A growth form of Candida albicans characterized by a unicellular morphology and cell cycle-dependent growth behavior. It is contrasted with pseudohyphae and true hyphae in the text.

A filamentous growth form of Candida albicans that differs from yeast and true hyphae in morphology and cell cycle progression. It is specifically mentioned as exhibiting polarized growth during cell cycle delay.
A filamentous growth form of Candida albicans associated with polarized, continuous elongation and altered coupling between growth and cell cycle events.
The ordered progression through cell cycle phases, discussed here in relation to morphogenesis and growth-form-specific regulation in Candida albicans.
Directional cellular growth toward a specific tip or axis, especially prominent in hyphal cells and also observed in yeast or pseudohyphae during cell cycle delay.
Continuous extension of hyphal cells, described as being directed by the Spitzenkörper in filamentous fungal species and Candida albicans hyphae.
The process of morphological development and shape change in Candida albicans, tightly linked to cell cycle progression and regulated by cyclins.
A temporary slowing or arrest-like delay in cell cycle progression that is associated with polarized growth in yeast or pseudohyphae.
An organelle composed of vesicles at hyphal tips that directs continuous hyphal elongation in filamentous fungi and Candida albicans hyphae.
Membrane-bound vesicular structures that compose the Spitzenkörper and contribute to tip-directed growth in hyphae.
Localized apical regions of hyphae where the Spitzenkörper is associated and where directional elongation is organized.
A polarity-related cellular complex that mediates cell cycle-dependent growth in yeast and pseudohyphae.
Cell cycle regulatory proteins that control morphogenesis and cell cycle progression, with some cyclins functioning specifically in yeast or hyphal cells.
Regulatory control points in the cell cycle that are proposed as future targets for understanding how morphogenesis is connected to cell cycle progression.
A broader fungal population context in which the Spitzenkörper directs continuous hyphal elongation; used as comparative biological context for Candida albicans.

A yeast species discussed as the organism in which the [GAR+] prion emerges and drives metabolic reprogramming. It serves as the microbial subject whose carbon metabolism is altered through interaction with bacterial cells in fermented-food contexts.

Bacterial microbial partners present in coculture with yeast and implicated in inducing the [GAR+] prion state. They function as interacting organisms that trigger yeast metabolic switching in mixed microbial communities.

A group of bacteria used in traditional sake making and described as participating in mutualistic symbiosis with yeasts. They are the bacterial population specifically linked to microbial communication and prion-mediated metabolic adaptation.

The food-production environment in which yeast-bacterial communities are observed, including products such as sourdough bread, cheese, kefir, wine, and sake. This setting provides the ecological and manufacturing context for microbial interactions.

A yeast prion state in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that is induced by coculturing with bacterial cells. It represents a molecular/epigenetic feature associated with altered carbon metabolism and metabolic reprogramming.
The metabolic process switched by emergence of the [GAR+] prion in yeast. It is the downstream biological process central to the reported metabolic reprogramming.

A cooperative interspecies interaction among microorganisms that is promoted by yeast-bacteria communication in traditional sake making. It reflects a beneficial ecological process supporting coexistence and metabolic adaptation.

The adaptive adjustment of microbial metabolism in cross-kingdom ecosystems, highlighted as a functional consequence of yeast prion-mediated communication. It captures the broader biological significance of the prion-driven switch.
Mixed microbial ecological systems containing both yeast and bacterial organisms. This context frames the interaction network in which prion-mediated metabolic reprogramming occurs.
Intercellular signaling and interaction among microorganisms in fermented-food communities. It is the broader process linking bacterial presence to yeast prion emergence and metabolic changes.

The overall process by which yeast prion formation alters metabolic state and adaptation. It integrates prion induction, carbon metabolism switching, and ecological interaction in fermented-food microbial communities.
A specific fermentation setting in which yeasts and lactic acid bacteria interact. It is the operational context where mutualistic symbiosis and prion-associated metabolic adaptation are described.

A polymorphic human fungal pathogen studied as the primary biological subject in this work. It includes laboratory strains and a clinical isolate, and is the organism whose virulence, morphogenesis, and ergosterol biosynthesis are evaluated in response to ganciclovir.

A reference strain of Candida albicans used as one of the test populations in the antifungal screening. It serves as an experimental subject for assessing ganciclovir effects on hyphal development and ergosterol biosynthesis.
A Candida albicans strain used in the study as a test population for evaluating the antifungal and anti-morphogenic activity of ganciclovir.
A clinical Candida albicans isolate included in the study to assess whether ganciclovir inhibits virulence-related phenotypes in non-reference pathogenic strains.
An in vivo experimental host model used to validate the virulence-inhibitory activity of ganciclovir against Candida albicans. It provides organism-level evidence beyond in vitro assays.

An antiviral drug repurposed and screened as an antifungal intervention in this study. It reduces hyphal development, suppresses ergosterol biosynthesis, and upregulates hyphal-specific repressors in Candida albicans.

A virulence-associated morphogenetic process in Candida albicans involving transition from yeast form to hyphal growth. It is a central biological process targeted by ganciclovir-mediated anti-morphogenic activity.
A virulence-related developmental process mentioned as a major aspect of Candida albicans pathogenicity. It is part of the broader antifungal target space discussed in the paper.
The formation and growth of hyphal structures in Candida albicans, representing a key morphogenetic and virulence process. The study reports partial inhibition of this process by ganciclovir.
A fungal sterol biosynthetic pathway essential for membrane integrity and fungal viability. The study reports concentration-dependent reduction of this process following ganciclovir treatment.
A hyphal-specific repressor gene/protein in Candida albicans whose expression is upregulated after ganciclovir treatment, suggesting a role in suppression of morphogenesis.
A hyphal-specific repressor in Candida albicans that is upregulated by ganciclovir treatment and is implicated in inhibition of yeast-to-hyphal transition.
A hyphal-specific repressor in Candida albicans whose expression increases after ganciclovir exposure, supporting anti-morphogenic effects.
A functional molecular category comprising MIG1, TUP1, and NRG1, which negatively regulate hyphal formation and are induced by ganciclovir.
The observed reduction in Candida albicans virulence-related phenotypes, supported by in vitro and in vivo findings after ganciclovir treatment.
An imaging method used to visualize the reduction in hyphal development on the silicon-based urinary catheter after ganciclovir treatment.

A biomaterial surface used as the observation context for hyphal development and antifungal activity assessment. It represents the device-associated environment where Candida albicans growth was visualized.

A broad population of disease-causing fungal organisms discussed as the biological subjects in which phenotypic variability, morphogenesis, and virulence are being studied. It serves as the overarching experimental/clinical population for the fungal examples in the abstract.

An experimental pathogenic fungal species used as a model to study phenotypic variability, switching, and virulence. The text emphasizes its controlled and programmed phenotypic changes and associated traits such as capsule, morphology, and virulence.

A dimorphic pathogenic fungal species discussed as a model organism for studying yeast-phase proteinase activity and fungal dissemination. It is used to illustrate how fungal enzymes may contribute to invasion and spread.

A pathogenic fungal species used as a model for examining adhesion, hyphal growth regulation, tropic responses, and invasive potential. It is central to the discussion of fungal pathogenicity mechanisms.

Variation in observable fungal traits that is linked to pathogenic behavior and virulence. In the text, it is described as a controlled and programmed process in Cryptococcus neoformans rather than random mutation-driven change.

The regulated developmental process by which fungi form distinct morphological states or phases. It is presented as a key mechanism underlying expression of regulated genes and disease-causing capacity.

A regulated biological switching process in Cryptococcus neoformans that replaces random mutation as the explanation for phenotypic variability. It reflects coordinated changes in fungal state and phenotype.
A fungal surface-associated molecular feature evaluated as a phenotypic trait in Cryptococcus neoformans. It is relevant to fungal morphology and virulence-associated properties.
The shape and structural form of fungal cells, assessed as a phenotypic trait in Cryptococcus neoformans. It is part of the morphological variability associated with virulence.
The macroscopic growth form of fungal colonies, evaluated as a phenotypic trait in Cryptococcus neoformans. It contributes to the characterization of phenotypic switching and pathogenic potential.
The capacity of a fungal organism to cause disease. In the abstract, virulence is a central endpoint correlated with phenotypic variability, morphogenesis, and specific fungal traits.
A fungal enzyme produced in the yeast phase of Paracoccidioides brasiliensis. It is implicated in cleavage of basal membrane components and may contribute to dissemination.
A morphological growth phase of Paracoccidioides brasiliensis in which the serine-thiol proteinase is expressed. It is relevant to fungal dimorphism and pathogenic behavior.

entity_name: MAIN COMPONENTS OF THE BASAL MEMBRANE
description: Structural molecular components of the basal membrane that are cleaved by the serine-thiol proteinase. Their degradation is relevant to tissue invasion and fungal dissemination.
The spread of fungal organisms through host tissues or beyond the initial site of infection. In the text, it is presented as a potential consequence of basal membrane cleavage by fungal proteinase.
Fungal surface or binding proteins involved in attachment interactions. In Candida albicans, they are discussed in relation to interactions with lymphocytes and neutrophils and to pathogenicity.
Host immune cells mentioned as interaction partners for fungal adhesion proteins. Their relationship to fungal adhesion is linked to pathogenicity in Candida albicans.
Host innate immune cells mentioned as interaction partners for fungal adhesion proteins. Their interaction with fungal adhesion proteins is associated with fungal pathogenicity.
The ability of fungal organisms to produce disease, used here as the broader pathogenic outcome associated with adhesion interactions and morphogenetic regulation.
The oriented growth process of fungal hyphae, which is regulated in Candida albicans. It is linked to tropic responses and invasive potential.
Directional response behaviors of fungal hyphae to environmental cues. In the abstract, these responses are correlated with invasive potential in Candida albicans.
The capacity of Candida albicans to invade host tissues. It is associated with regulation of hyphal directional growth and tropic responses.

A fungal pathogen studied as the biological subject in this paper. It is the organism in which Efg1 regulation, filamentation, biofilm formation, and virulence are examined, and it serves as the experimental model for the reported genetic manipulations and infection studies.

A master transcriptional regulator in Candida albicans that controls filamentation and hyphal morphogenesis. The study tests whether its function depends on phosphorylation at T208 by protein kinase A and evaluates its role in filamentation, biofilm formation, gene expression, and virulence.

A signaling pathway long proposed to phosphorylate Efg1 and drive filamentation in Candida albicans. In this study, it is the mechanistic pathway being reassessed for its role in regulating hyphal morphogenesis and related virulence traits.

A post-translational regulatory process proposed to modify Efg1 at T208. The paper evaluates whether this phosphorylation event is required for filamentation, biofilm formation, and infection-related phenotypes.

The putative protein kinase A phosphorylation site on Efg1 that was mutated to Ala or Glu in the engineered strains. It is the focal molecular residue used to test the phosphorylation-dependent regulation model.

The yeast-to-filament transition and formation of filamentous growth forms in Candida albicans. This process is central to the organism's morphogenesis and virulence and is used as a primary functional readout in the study.
The developmental process by which Candida albicans forms hyphae. It is the broader morphogenetic context in which Efg1 regulation is investigated and is linked to pathogenicity.

The process by which Candida albicans forms structured surface-associated communities. The study assesses whether Efg1 phosphorylation status affects this phenotype as part of its functional analysis.
Transcriptional output measured during in vitro filamentation to determine whether Efg1 phosphorylation influences downstream regulatory programs. It serves as a molecular readout of Efg1 function.

The pathogenic capacity of Candida albicans, assessed in an experimental model of disseminated candidiasis. It is a key disease-relevant endpoint used to determine whether Efg1 phosphorylation affects infection severity.
An invasive Candida infection model used to evaluate virulence in vivo. It provides the disease context for testing whether Efg1 phosphorylation is required for pathogenicity.
Filament formation studied under laboratory inducing conditions. It is used as a functional assay context to test the effect of Efg1 phosphorylation mutants across a wide range of conditions.
Filament formation occurring within a living host or infection context. It is one of the phenotypes assessed to determine whether Efg1 phosphorylation affects morphogenesis during infection.

Candida albicans mutant strains lacking EFG1, used as the genetic background into which phosphorylation-site alleles were integrated. They function as engineered experimental subjects for testing Efg1-dependent phenotypes.
Engineered Candida albicans strains containing modified EFG1 alleles. These strains are the experimental models used to evaluate the functional consequences of blocking or mimicking phosphorylation.
Genetically engineered variants of the EFG1 locus introduced into mutant strains. They encode altered phosphorylation states at T208 and are central to the study's mechanistic test.
The amino acid substitution used to block phosphorylation at Efg1 T208. It represents the non-phosphorylatable mutant state in the engineered alleles.
The amino acid substitution used to mimic phosphorylation at Efg1 T208. It represents the phosphomimetic mutant state in the engineered alleles.

Genetic engineering and strain construction methods used to create and analyze EFG1 phosphorylation-site mutants. These approaches provide the experimental basis for reassessing the protein kinase A-Efg1 paradigm.

The laboratory conditions under which in vitro filamentation was induced and tested. This setting is important because the historical phosphorylation model was previously reported to apply only to specific in vitro conditions.
The infection setting in which virulence was assessed. It provides the in vivo context for evaluating the pathogenic consequences of Efg1 phosphorylation mutants.

Budding yeast organism used as the biological subject in the study of morphogenetic transition and signaling regulation. It is the population in which pseudohyphal growth, InsP signaling, and mutant phenotypes are examined.

A filamentous morphological transition in yeast characterized by elongated cells remaining connected post-cytokinesis in multicellular pseudohyphae. It is the central biological process being regulated and analyzed in relation to inositol polyphosphate signaling and kinase pathways.

The differentiated growth state in which yeast cells adopt elongated, connected filament-like morphology. It represents the morphological outcome of pseudohyphal development under inducing conditions.
A conserved cellular organization process that contributes to directional growth and morphogenesis. In this context, it is one of the pathways enabling pseudohyphal filament formation.
The standard yeast growth mode involving asymmetric cell division. It is contrasted with pseudohyphal growth as the classic growth mode from which cells transition.
The arrangement and remodeling of cytoskeletal structures that support morphological change. It is part of the signaling network enabling pseudohyphal growth.
The process by which cells adhere to one another, supporting multicellular filament formation. It is implicated in the pseudohyphal growth transition.

Second messenger molecules involved in regulating pseudohyphal growth and broader cellular signaling. They are generated from phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate and show condition-dependent profiles during filamentation.
Abbreviation for inositol polyphosphates, functioning as soluble second messengers. They are highlighted as regulators of pseudohyphal growth and other diverse processes.
Membrane-bound phosphoinositide precursor cleaved to form inositol polyphosphates. It is the upstream molecular substrate in the InsP signaling pathway.
Abbreviation for phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate, the membrane lipid precursor of inositol polyphosphates. It links membrane phosphoinositide metabolism to second messenger production.
Enzymes in the inositol polyphosphate pathway required for wild-type pseudohyphal growth. They are functionally important regulators of InsP production and signaling output.
Distinct molecular forms of inositol polyphosphates whose abundance profiles change under filamentation-promoting conditions. They serve as readouts of pathway state and regulatory balance.
A doubly phosphorylated InsP7 isoform whose ratio relative to 1PP-InsP5 is elevated in mutants with exaggerated pseudohyphal growth. It is a specific molecular marker of altered InsP metabolism.
A doubly phosphorylated InsP7 isoform used in ratio comparisons with 5PP-InsP5. Its relative abundance helps characterize mutant InsP profiles associated with enhanced pseudohyphal growth.
A conserved kinase family implicated in signaling control of InsP levels and pseudohyphal regulation. In this study context, the family includes Kss1p and Fus3p as relevant members.
A yeast MAPK whose deletion produces mutant InsP profiles. It is implicated in the signaling network that may regulate inositol polyphosphate levels and pseudohyphal growth.
A yeast MAPK whose deletion alters InsP profiles. It is part of the conserved signaling machinery potentially contributing to regulation of InsP-mediated morphogenesis.
A conserved energy-sensing kinase family implicated in the regulation of InsP levels. It is discussed as a signaling component influencing pseudohyphal-associated InsP profiles.
A yeast AMPK family member whose deletion causes mutant InsP profiles. It is a key signaling protein linking metabolic state to regulation of inositol polyphosphate signaling and morphogenesis.
The external environmental conditions that trigger the yeast morphological transition. They provide the context in which pseudohyphal growth is initiated.
Experimental or environmental conditions that favor the filamentous pseudohyphal state. These conditions are associated with characteristic InsP species profiles.
A diverse cellular process mentioned as one of the broader functions regulated by inositol polyphosphates. It provides functional context for the signaling role of InsPs beyond yeast morphogenesis.
A cellular regulatory process cited as being influenced by inositol polyphosphates. It indicates broader metabolic significance of InsP signaling.
Stress-adaptation processes that may be modulated by conserved second messengers such as InsPs. The text suggests pseudohyphal growth analyses may reveal mechanisms relevant to these responses.

A pathogenic yeast species serving as the central biological subject of the review. It is described as an opportunistic human pathogen, clinically relevant in nosocomial infections, and also as a non-conventional model organism for studying cellular physiology, morphogenesis, and genome maintenance.

A vulnerable patient population frequently associated with nosocomial infections caused by Candida parapsilosis. They represent a clinically important host stratum with diminished immunity and heightened susceptibility to infection.

An immunocompromised patient population noted as frequently affected by Candida parapsilosis-associated nosocomial infections. This group is relevant because reduced immune function increases susceptibility to opportunistic fungal disease.
Hospital-acquired infections associated with Candida parapsilosis in neonates and immunocompromised patients. This is the main clinical outcome emphasized in the abstract.

Research approaches and enabling methodologies used to study the molecular basis of Candida parapsilosis virulence. In this context, they provide the analytical foundation for uncovering pathogenic mechanisms and supporting genetic investigation.

The underlying biological mechanisms that enable Candida parapsilosis pathogenicity and disease-causing capacity. The abstract highlights this as a key research target revealed by modern molecular studies.
Potential treatment strategies aimed at countering Candida parapsilosis infection or virulence. The text presents this as a promising application of insights gained from molecular studies.

Distinct biological characteristics of Candida parapsilosis that are absent in model yeasts. These features are important because they distinguish the species from conventional models and motivate its use in fundamental research.
A conventional yeast model organism referenced for comparison. It is used as a contrast class to emphasize that Candida parapsilosis has features absent from standard yeast models.
Another conventional yeast model organism referenced for comparison. It serves as a benchmark against which Candida parapsilosis is described as biologically distinct.
The role assigned to Candida parapsilosis as a research model outside the standard baker's and fission yeast systems. This status reflects its utility for studying fundamental biological phenomena.
A fundamental biological process area identified as a research focus enabled by Candida parapsilosis as a model organism. It encompasses cellular function and regulation.
The biological process of form and structure development in Candida parapsilosis. It is highlighted as one of the fundamental phenomena suitable for investigation in this species.
The biological process of preserving genome integrity and stability in Candida parapsilosis. It is specifically mentioned as a fundamental phenomenon that can be studied using this organism.

Experimental approaches used to alter Candida parapsilosis genetically for research purposes. These methods have improved the ability to study the species by overcoming limitations of conventional genetic analysis.

Conventional analytical approaches for studying genetic properties of Candida parapsilosis. The abstract notes that these approaches were limited by the organism's biology, motivating improved manipulation methods.
A biological characteristic of Candida parapsilosis that limits conventional genetic analysis. This feature is important because it constrains classical breeding-based genetic approaches.

The diploid genomic condition of Candida parapsilosis, identified as a factor complicating conventional genetic analysis. It is a key genomic attribute relevant to experimental manipulation and inheritance patterns.

Human pathogenic yeast used as the biological subject in the study. It undergoes morphogen-induced transitions between yeast, pseudomycelial, mycelial, and chlamydospore forms, making it the central organism for the observed developmental responses.

A morphogenic effector and carbon source that induces morphogenesis in Candida albicans. It functions as both an inducer of yeast-mycelial conversion and chlamydospore formation, and is implicated in receptor-mediated signaling that primes morphogenesis.

A glucose analog that acts as a potent inhibitor of N-acetylglucosamine-induced germ-tube formation at concentrations that do not impair yeast growth. It is used to probe the specificity of the morphogenic response.

An environmental condition that modulates the developmental response of Candida albicans to N-acetylglucosamine. Higher temperatures favor germ-tube and yeast-mycelial conversion, whereas lower temperatures favor yeast or pseudomycelial forms.
A morphogenetic transition in Candida albicans from yeast form to mycelial form. It is induced by N-acetylglucosamine and requires transcription and translation.
A developmental morphogenetic process induced by N-acetylglucosamine in Candida albicans, representing an alternative differentiation outcome under specific conditions.

General proliferative growth of Candida albicans in the yeast form, supported by N-acetylglucosamine as a carbon source and not significantly affected by 2-deoxyglucose at the concentrations described.

An intermediary morphogenetic process in yeast-mycelial conversion characterized by germ-tube emergence. It is induced by N-acetylglucosamine at temperatures above 33 degrees C and is inhibited by 2-deoxyglucose.
A gene expression process required for N-acetylglucosamine-induced yeast-to-mycelial transition in Candida albicans, indicating that new RNA synthesis is necessary for morphogenesis.
A protein synthesis process required for N-acetylglucosamine-induced yeast-to-mycelial transition in Candida albicans, indicating dependence on new protein production.
The cellular transport process by which Candida albicans acquires N-acetylglucosamine. Enzymes involved in uptake are induced similarly in yeast-phase and germ-tube-forming cells.
The metabolic breakdown of N-acetylglucosamine in Candida albicans. Enzymes for catabolism are induced by gene expression in both yeast-phase and germ-tube-forming cells.
A structural molecular feature of the fungal cell wall that increases during germ-tube formation, reflecting remodeling associated with morphogenesis.
A regulatory enzyme whose activity increases during germ-tube formation in Candida albicans, linking cell wall biosynthesis to morphogenetic transition.

A group of compounds, including N-acetylglucosamine covalently linked to agarose, N-acetylmannosamine, hyaluronic acid, colloidal chitin, and mucin, that can gratuitously induce germ-tube formation without being taken up or supporting growth.
A proposed receptor-mediated sensing mechanism at the cell surface that triggers germ-tube formation in response to N-acetylhexosamine derivatives and N-acetylglucosamine binding.
A proposed intracellular signaling message generated after N-acetylglucosamine binding to a receptor, which primes Candida albicans for morphogenesis and determines growth mode choice.

The developmental process by which Candida albicans changes form, including yeast-mycelial conversion and germ-tube formation. It is induced by N-acetylglucosamine and influenced by temperature and receptor-mediated signaling.
A morphological growth state of Candida albicans characterized by spherical growth and predominance at lower temperatures. It serves as one of the alternative developmental outcomes in the study.

A morphological growth state of Candida albicans characterized by apical growth and associated with the yeast-mycelial transition. It represents the filamentous outcome promoted by N-acetylglucosamine under inducing conditions.
An alternative morphological state of Candida albicans that predominates at lower temperatures when germ-tube-inducing conditions are absent or reduced.

The regulation of Ace2 and morphogenesis (RAM) network is a conserved protein kinase signaling pathway in eukaryotes. In this text it functions as a central biological process controlling fungal development, morphogenesis, cell-cycle-linked events, and stress responses, with relevance to both model yeast and pathogenic fungi.

Ace2 is a molecular component named in the RAM network acronym and is associated with regulation of morphogenesis and gene expression in fungi. It is part of the pathway context described in the paper and helps define the signaling network's functional identity.

Morphogenesis is a biological process involving the development of cellular form and structure. In this abstract it is explicitly linked to the RAM network, which regulates fungal morphogenetic programs.

A signaling pathway mediated by protein kinases. The RAM network is described as a conserved protein kinase signaling pathway, indicating its mechanistic basis in phosphorylation-dependent signal transduction.
The broad biological population across which the RAM network is conserved, spanning yeasts to humans. It provides the evolutionary context for the pathway's conservation.
A fungal population stratum used as part of the evolutionary and comparative context for the RAM network. The pathway is described as conserved from yeasts to humans.
The human population is mentioned as the upper end of the conservation range for the RAM network, indicating broad evolutionary preservation of the pathway.
A model yeast species in which the RAM network has been most extensively studied. It serves as the primary experimental model for understanding RAM network function in fungi.
A regulated cellular process in which genes are expressed specifically in daughter cells. The RAM network is reported to control this process in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
The control of progression through the cell cycle. The RAM network is described as regulating this process in fungal cells.
The biological process by which daughter cells separate after division. It is one of the cellular processes regulated by the RAM network.
A reproductive biological process in fungi. The RAM network is reported to regulate mating in the model yeast context.
Directional cell growth that establishes cellular polarity. The RAM network is described as regulating polarized growth in fungi.
A protective cellular process that preserves fungal cell wall structure and function. The RAM network contributes to this process, linking signaling to structural homeostasis.
Cellular signaling responses to environmental or physiological stress. The RAM network is reported to regulate stress signaling in fungi.
The biological process by which organisms cause disease. The RAM network is stated to play an important role in fungal pathogenesis.
A broad fungal population category encompassing the pathogenic species discussed in the paper. It provides the organismal context for RAM network function.
Fungal species capable of causing disease. The paper focuses on RAM network function in these pathogenic organisms and their biology/pathogenesis.
A human fungal pathogen discussed as one of the pathogenic species in which RAM network function has been studied. It is relevant as a disease-causing fungal organism.
A human fungal pathogen included among the species used to summarize recent developments in RAM network function. It is part of the pathogenic fungal context.
A human fungal pathogen discussed in relation to RAM network function and pathogenesis. It represents one of the pathogenic fungal species of interest.
A human fungal pathogen included in the summary of RAM network studies. It is relevant as a pathogenic fungal species with disease-causing potential.
A group of Pneumocystis species discussed as human fungal pathogens in the context of RAM network function. It represents a pathogenic fungal population relevant to disease biology.

The fungal pathogen studied as the biological subject of the paper. It is the organism in which Ent2-mediated morphogenesis, filamentation, and virulence are investigated, including its ability to switch between yeast and filamentous growth states.

An in vivo experimental model used to assess virulence of Candida albicans. It represents the host population in which Ent2 and its ENTH domain were tested for their role in systemic infection and disease severity.

A morphological developmental process in Candida albicans involving transition to filamentous/hyphal forms. It is critical for virulence and is shown here to require Ent2 under multiple inducing conditions.

Alternative morphological growth programs in Candida albicans. The transition between these states is described as essential for pathogenicity and is the broader developmental switch regulated by genes such as Ent2.
The developmental process governing shape and structural transitions in Candida albicans. In this study, Ent2 is characterized as a core regulator of morphogenesis, particularly hyphal morphogenesis.
The specific morphogenetic program leading to hyphal growth in Candida albicans. It is the process directly regulated by Ent2 through the Cdc42 signaling cascade.
The pathogenic capacity of Candida albicans to cause disease. The paper shows that Ent2 and its ENTH domain are required for virulence in a mouse model of systemic candidiasis.
A disseminated fungal infection caused by Candida albicans. It is the disease endpoint used in the in vivo mouse model to evaluate the contribution of Ent2 to pathogenicity.
A fungal protein identified as a core regulator of morphogenesis and virulence in Candida albicans. It functions through its ENTH domain and interacts with Rga2 to influence Cdc42-Cla4 signaling.
The epsin N-terminal homology domain of Ent2. This domain is specifically required for morphogenesis and virulence and mediates the functional interaction with Rga2.

A Cdc42 regulatory protein that interacts physically with Ent2. Its localization is regulated by Ent2, and this interaction is important for proper activation of downstream signaling involved in morphogenesis.
A downstream effector in the Cdc42 signaling pathway. Overexpression of Cla4 can bypass the requirement for the Ent2-ENTH/Rga2 interaction, indicating its functional position downstream of Ent2.
A signaling cascade downstream of Cdc42 that promotes morphogenetic transitions in Candida albicans. Ent2 contributes to proper activation of this pathway in response to filament-inducing cues.
An inducing condition or environmental cue that promotes filamentation in Candida albicans. The study notes that Ent2 supports pathway activation in the presence of such cues.
A broad set of experimental conditions used to trigger filamentous growth in Candida albicans. Ent2 is required for filamentous growth across a wide range of these conditions.

An opportunistic human fungal pathogen studied as the biological subject in this paper. It is the organism whose morphogenesis, filamentation, and virulence are being regulated by DYRK-family kinases and the Ras1/PKA pathway.
A human population stratum described as highly susceptible to life-threatening Candida albicans infections. This population provides the clinical context for the pathogen's virulence relevance.

entity_name: MOUSE MODEL OF C. ALBICANS DERMATITIS
description: An experimental mouse disease model used to test the requirement of Yak1 for filamentation in vivo. It serves as the host/subject context for assessing fungal virulence-related phenotypes under genetic and pharmacological manipulation.

An environmental gas exposure scenario reflecting host-like carbon dioxide levels that influence fungal morphogenesis. In this context, CO2 bypasses the requirement for Yak1 during Candida albicans morphogenesis.
A conserved signaling pathway implicated in regulating Candida albicans morphogenesis and filamentation. The paper shows Yak1 regulates morphogenesis through this pathway.
A signaling pathway referenced in the title as the mechanism through which DYRK-family kinases regulate morphogenesis and virulence. It is central to fungal morphogenetic control.
The developmental process by which Candida albicans transitions between morphological states. It is a key regulated process in the study and is linked to virulence.
The transition to filamentous growth in Candida albicans, a major virulence-associated developmental process. The study examines its regulation by Yak1 and Pom1 under different conditions.
Alternative morphological states between which Candida albicans transitions. This switching underlies morphogenesis and contributes to pathogenicity.
The disease-causing capacity of Candida albicans, discussed as an important pathogenic endpoint. The title and abstract link DYRK-family kinase regulation to virulence.
A severe clinical outcome caused by Candida albicans in immunocompromised individuals. This endpoint motivates the study of fungal virulence mechanisms.
The observed growth phenotype corresponding to filamentation. In the study, deletion of both Yak1 and Pom1 blocked filamentous growth under all tested conditions.
A kinase in Candida albicans that regulates filamentation and morphogenesis. It acts through the canonical cAMP/PKA pathway and is required for filamentation in the mouse dermatitis model.
A related kinase that contributes to filamentation when Yak1 is absent under host-relevant CO2 conditions. It functions as a compensatory regulator of fungal morphogenesis.
A kinase family highlighted in the title as regulators of Candida albicans morphogenesis and virulence. Yak1 and Pom1 are the specific family members discussed in the abstract.
Experimental intervention strategies used to test Yak1 function in the mouse dermatitis model. These approaches alter fungal regulatory pathways to assess effects on filamentation.

The insect host organism studied in the paper. It is the population whose larval development rate, feeding behavior, and microbiota-dependent growth were compared under axenic versus microbiota-associated conditions.

A microbe-free Drosophila melanogaster experimental population reared without associated microbes. This population serves as the key comparison group for assessing how absence of gut microbes affects development time and growth.
The normal microbial community associated with Drosophila melanogaster. It represents the microbiota-bearing condition associated with faster egg-to-adult development relative to axenic flies.

The developmental stage of Drosophila melanogaster examined for yeast inoculation, feeding changes, and developmental acceleration. Larvae are the primary stage in which yeast-mediated effects on growth and development were assessed.

Viable yeast organisms introduced into the fly gut or larval environment. They function as beneficial symbionts that restore fast development in axenic flies and increase feeding rate during later larval development.
A single live yeast species used to inoculate larvae. It is one of the yeast agents shown to restore the faster development phenotype in axenic Drosophila melanogaster.
A single live yeast species used to inoculate larvae. It is the second yeast agent reported to restore accelerated development in axenic Drosophila melanogaster.
Non-viable yeast preparations used as a nutritional supplement. They slightly accelerated development of axenic flies but were less effective than live yeasts.

entity_name: MIX OF ESSENTIAL VITAMINS AND AMINO ACIDS
description: A nutritional supplement composed of essential vitamins and amino acids. It modestly sped development in axenic flies, indicating that nutrient availability contributes to the observed developmental acceleration.

The broader microbial community residing in insect guts. In the paper, it is the ecological context in which yeast-host interactions are discussed, with emphasis on its role in host physiology, performance, and behavior.

The anatomical environment where microbial communities reside and interact with the host. This setting is central to the observed presence and reproduction of live yeasts and their effects on host development.
The developmental endpoint measured as total time from egg to adult emergence. It is the primary outcome used to compare developmental speed across microbial and yeast treatment conditions.

The duration required for Drosophila melanogaster to progress through development. It is shortened by live yeasts and modestly by nutritional supplements, serving as the main phenotypic endpoint in the study.
The rate at which larvae consume food during development. It increased in the third instar in response to live yeasts, suggesting a behavioral mechanism contributing to accelerated growth.

The availability of major nutritional resources supporting growth and development. The paper proposes that additional macronutrients from live yeasts contribute to faster development during the first two larval instars.

A host signaling pathway linking gut status to feeding behavior and developmental regulation. The study suggests that live yeasts may accelerate development during the third instar through this mechanism.

Early larval developmental stages of Drosophila melanogaster. These stages are identified as the period during which yeast-associated acceleration appears to be driven by additional macronutrient availability.
The later larval developmental stage in Drosophila melanogaster when most growth occurs. In this stage, live yeasts increased feeding rate, implying a gut-brain-axis-mediated effect.
The fungal pathogen studied in the paper; it serves as the biological subject in which CaNrg1 function, hyphal morphogenesis, gene repression, stress sensitivity, and virulence are examined.

A Candida albicans transcriptional regulator containing a conserved zinc finger domain; it functions as a transcriptional repressor that controls hypha-specific genes, virulence-related functions, and yeast-hypha morphogenesis.
A Saccharomyces cerevisiae Nrg1 homolog mentioned as the closest relative of CaNrg1; it represses transcription in a Tup1-dependent manner and provides comparative functional context.
A transcriptional corepressor referenced as a functional partner in repression; CaNrg1 represses a subset of CaTup1-regulated genes and appears to target CaTup1 to virulence-related functions.
A subset of genes regulated by CaTup1 that are repressed by CaNrg1; this set includes hypha-specific genes and other virulence-associated genes.
Genes expressed in hyphal growth programs that are derepressed upon CaNrg1 inactivation; they are part of the morphogenesis and virulence regulatory network.
Genes or gene products associated with pathogenicity that are included among the CaNrg1-repressed targets and contribute to Candida albicans virulence.
A promoter DNA element recognized by CaNrg1; most CaNrg1-repressed genes contain this element, and its presence is required for Nrg1-mediated repression.
The promoter region of ALS8 used as a specific regulatory example; deletion of two NREs from this promoter relieves repression by CaNrg1.
An altered growth program observed after CaNrg1 inactivation in C. albicans, reflecting enhanced filamentation and tissue-invasive behavior.
The developmental transition between yeast and hyphal forms in Candida albicans; CaNrg1 represses this process and thereby influences pathogenic morphology.
The gene-expression process regulated by Nrg1-family repressors; ScNrg1 is described as repressing transcription in a Tup1-dependent fashion.
The expression program of hyphal genes that is repressed by CaNrg1 and derepressed upon its inactivation.
A phenotypic outcome increased in CaNrg1-inactivated cells, indicating altered tolerance to environmental stresses.
The pathogenicity-related outcome attenuated by CaNrg1 inactivation and linked to regulation of virulence factors and morphogenesis.
A morphological developmental outcome that nrg1 cells can form at normal rates, indicating that this phenotype is not impaired by CaNrg1 loss.
A temperature-growth phenotype retained in nrg1 cells; it serves as a specific physiological endpoint distinguishing nrg1 from tup1 mutants.
A conserved DNA-binding domain present in CaNrg1 and related transcriptional regulators, supporting its role in sequence-specific promoter recognition.
A mechanistic regulatory framework describing how ScNrg1 represses transcription through dependence on Tup1; included as a functional mode of action rather than a quantitative metric.
